0003-2026.title: Petition 0003/2026: Regulation (EC) No 261/2004
0003-2026.description_full: The petitioner points out that Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 regulates passenger compensation in the event of delays. Article 12 speaks of "crediting" to further claims. However, according to the petitioner, it is completely unclear whether the compensation for "inconvenience" also covers concrete material damage. The petitioner describes the case, with flight delay during the package tour, and points out that experts had different opinions on the crediting of claims. According to the petitioner, the consequences of the ambiguities are that tour operators systematically refuse payments and consumers remain seated on damages. The petitioner asks the European Parliament to clarify in Article 12 of Regulation 261/2004 that compensation for intangible damage (stress, waiting time) is not to be counted towards material damage (not received hotel services, local taxes). According to the petitioner, this would strengthen consumer protection and ensure fair burden-sharing between airlines and organisers.

1554-2025.title: Petition 1554/2025: an alleged infringement of the Digital Services Act by Meta
1554-2025.description_full: The petitioner denounces that her Instagram account was suspended for alleged adult sexual services. According to the petitioner, this is a false accusation. The petitioner argues that META has infringed the Digital Services Act by inadequately reasoning the content restriction, defective internal complaint-handling system and taking over 8 days without processing appeal. The petitioner considers that this situation affects millions of European citizens facing arbitrary account suspensions by Meta platforms. According to the petitioner, Meta systematically violates DSA requirements for transparent content moderation, effective appeal processes and timely complaint handling. The petitioner urges the European Parliament to investigate Meta's alleged systematic DSA violations, impose significant penalties under DSA Article 74, demand immediate compliance with EU law and protect European citizens from arbitrary platform decisions.

1386-2024.title: Petition 1386/2024: alleged insufficient implementation of Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 by Germany
1386-2024.description_full: The petitioner, a German civil servant residing in Switzerland, raises concerns about alleged gaps in the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 883/2004 on the coordination of social security systems into German law. Despite being privately insured in Germany prior to relocation, the petitioner faced challenges when his insurer limited coverage in Switzerland and required a premium surcharge. The petitioner could not obtain insurance from Swiss providers due to ongoing employment in Germany nor from German public health insurance schemes. Attempts to secure coverage with another private insurer also failed due to the change in residence to Switzerland. The petitioner argues that the German law inadequately reflects the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 883/2004, particularly for civil servants, as the regulation applies to EFTA states, including Switzerland. Unlike Norway, Iceland, and Liechtenstein, Switzerland is not covered under the German law, creating an alleged legal gap. Efforts to resolve the issue with the Ombudsman for Private Health Insurance and the Federal Financial Supervisory Authority (BaFin) were unsuccessful.

0919-2024.title: Petition 0919/2024: linguistic diversity and accessibility on streaming platforms in the EU
0919-2024.category: Internal Market - Free movement of goods and services
0919-2024.description_full: The petitioner says that streaming platforms should have to provide access to Polish versions of streaming materials across the European Union. According to the petitioner, platforms such as Netflix do not offer Polish language streaming in Germany despite the same materials being available in Poland, in Polish. The petitioner claims that this limits Polish children living abroad who are unable to view materials in their native language: this in turn infringes on their cultural identity and the parents’ ability to educate. The petitioner calls for the introduction of regulations to require streaming platforms to make materials available in all languages of the European Union. According to the petitioner, this change would align with the ethos of both EU and UN law, which it currently contradicts with regard to equal access to media and culture.

0734-2024.description_full: The petitioner highlights an alleged lack of accessibility for wheelchair users in Germany and across the EU, pointing out that many public spaces, including train stations, buses, and rural stops, are not barrier-free. The petitioner argues that there should be regulations at both the national and EU levels to improve accessibility. This includes ensuring that all new buses, trains, and public buildings are fully accessible, eliminating barriers such as stairs, narrow doorways, and lack of elevators. The petitioner calls for swift action to improve the everyday freedom and mobility of people with disabilities.

0733-2024.title: Petition 0733/2024
0733-2024.description_full: The petitioner points out that testing on European waters has revealed high concentrations of PFAS degradation products, such as trifluoroacetate (TFA). According to the petitioner, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) does not consider that TFAs pose a risk, therefore no monitoring obligations or limit values are in place. The petitioner states that these degradation products and PFAS could make their way into groundwater, which could threaten to compromise drinking water. The petitioner states that it is therefore necessary to restrict PFAS under the REACH Regulation, to make the Water Framework Directive’s provisions on TFAs more stringent and to establish limits values and monitoring obligations for PFAS. The petitioner is also in favour of banning non-essential uses of PFAS.

0861-2023.description_full: According to the petitioner, the national compensation procedures for victims of sexual violence in Germany violate the European Convention on Human Rights, as well as the European Victims' Rights Directive. The petitioner states as reasons, among others, the consequences of retraumatisation and secondary victimisation during the proceedings, which the petitioner allegedly experienced during the processing of his petition by the Committee on Petitions of the German Land of Baden-Württemberg. According to the petitioner, the communication with the authorities, the medical assessments, the court proceedings and the processing time of the petitioner's application for victim compensation have led to further damage to his health. The petitioner states that many other victims have similar traumatising experiences in Germany, which all violate the European Victims' Rights Directive.

0855-2022.title: Petition 0855/2022: the impact of sanctions against Russia on German citizens
0855-2022.description_full: The petitioner has submitted the petition on behalf of his wife, who is originally from Russia and has been a German citizen for ten years, and stresses how she is directly affected by the sanctions – most notably the SWIFT-related sanctions – imposed by the EU on Russia. The petitioner explains that his wife made contributions to the Russian pension system and usually receives a pension from her country of origin. However, since the sanctions were imposed on Russia, she has not been able to access her pension as it is not possible via a German bank. The petitioner’s wife has lost her income as a result of the sanctions, which he regards as a violation of EU citizens’ human rights and fundamental freedoms. The petitioner regrets that precautions to avoid such problems were not taken in the planning phase prior to the implementation of the sanctions. The petitioner calls on the EU to address this issue as a matter of international law and to consider ways of providing compensation.

0527-2022.title: Petition 0527/2022: alleged violations of EU public procurement law in Germany
0527-2022.description_full: The petitioner calls on the Commission to take action against a widespread public procurement practice in Germany, which is preventing the best talent from having a fair shot in planning competitions. According to the petitioner, preference is given to running restricted competitions in Germany. He claims that random selection is used to reduce the number of participants. This is done on the basis of a special provision in Section 75(6) of the German Ordinance on the Award of Public Contracts, which allows for a selection to be made by drawing lots ‘if the number of applicants is too high even following an objective selection process pursuant to the underlying eligibility criteria’. That special provision has no equivalent in Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement, which in recital 93 states that the drawing of lots should be avoided. What is more, preferred architects and planning agencies are allegedly pre-selected prior to the lots being drawn and are as such allowed to participate without being part of the random selection. This unfair practice places applicants from other Member States at a disadvantage. To demonstrate what he describes, the petitioner provides a specific example of a planning competition that was run for Hamburg train station.

1209-2021.title: Petition 1209/2021: the situation of EU citizen Luis Frometa Compte in Cuba
1209-2021.description_full: The petitioner urges the European Parliament to take concrete measures to pursue the freedom of Mr Luis Frómeta Compte, who is imprisoned in Cuba and for whom the Cuban prosecution demands 24 years of imprisonment. Mr Compte is an EU citizen, who was on a family visit to Cuba in July 2021, when some anti-government riots took place. Mr Compte was filming the events on the street with his smartphone, when he was forcibly taken to the police station by the competent authorities and was later arrested. According to the petitioner, the charges against Mr Compte are unjustifiable and arbitrary, reflecting the injustice of a totalitarian regime. Therefore, he calls on the European Parliament to help Mr Compte and stand with the other political prisoners in Cuba, who are subject to the harsh injustice of the national regime.

0435-2021.title: Petition 0435/2021: the right to leave and return to Cuba.
0435-2021.started_by: M. S. G. B. (Cuban), bearing 6 000 signatures,
0435-2021.description_full: The petitioner writes about the situation of Cubans residing in the EU. Following enactment in Cuba of Law No 989 in 1962, the Cuban authorities identified the act of emigrating from the country as ‘treason’, for which an exit permit was necessary. The latter only ceased to be necessary when the migration reform of 2013 was brought in. The UN states that there are currently around 1 654 684 people with Cuban nationality living outside the country (14 % of the population), including approximately 200 000 residents of countries in the European Community, mainly in Spain, Italy, Germany and France, many of them with refugee status. As residents or citizens of the European Union, they ask Parliament to adopt a resolution condemning the human rights violations in Cuba and consider that these practices by the Cuban State also entail a violation of its commitments vis-à-vis the European Union as part of the EU-Cuba Political Dialogue and Cooperation Agreement in 2017. They ask for the support of the international community and the United Nations in order to drive forward a national reconciliation process.

1563-2020.title: Petition 1563/2020: protection of wolves under the Habitats Directive
1563-2020.description_full: The petitioner indicates that the co-signatory, who keeps sheep, is contributing with his flock to dyke maintenance. Between April 2019 and September 2020, however, he lost 460 sheep to wolf attacks and is now seriously thinking of abandoning his activity. Without dyke maintenance by sheep farmers, dyke safety and flood protection could no longer be guaranteed. DNA samples have identified the wolves in the pack that are responsible for the killing the sheep. The petitioner is accordingly seeking official accreditation for independent DNA sampling laboratories across Europe, the introduction of a joint European Canis Lupus gene database and, finally, a change in the protection status of wolves.

0891-2020.title: Petition 0891/2020
0891-2020.description_full: The petitioner denounces the actions of both, the main financial control body in Germany (Federal Financial Supervisory Authority BaFin), and the German public prosecutor’s office, which initiated proceedings to sanction complainants for market manipulation, in a possible accounting fraud by the Wirecard company between 2008 and 2016. In February 2019, BaFin prohibited short selling of Wirecard shares, alleging market manipulation by complainants and Financial Times journalists. BaFin justified the measure citing the wish to avoid a loss of investor confidence. The petitioner points out that in June 2020 it was discovered that all allegations against Wirecard were true and that there were also illegal activities by Wirecard which had not yet been reported. The petitioner considers that Bafin’s measures in fact caused exactly what it said it was trying to prevent, a manipulation of the market price. It also caused investors to place trust in the company unjustifiably. It is estimated that 250 000 small European investors were affected by massive damage to their savings and pension schemes as a result. The damage caused to these investors is estimated to be close to EUR 20 000 million. The petitioner asks the European Parliament to discuss and assess the role of the German administrations in the Wirecard fraud and to seek a solution for the small investors affected who now have to deal with an economy affected by Covid19, with massive losses in their savings.

0499-2020.title: Petition 0499/2020: the different kinds of European nitrate measuring systems
0499-2020.description_full: The petitioner claims that, as a result of the review of the Fertilisers Regulation, the transposition of the Nitrates Directive has been delayed by several years. In his opinion, however, there are problems with the measurement systems across the EU, as the measuring stations in the Member States do not use the same standards and thus results cannot easily be compared. 1342-2015.title: Petition 1342/2015: serious deficiencies in a fishing vessel that were discovered after purchase
1342-2015.description_full: The petitioner is an Irish fisherman who bought a fishing vessel in the Netherlands in 2007. The vessel was registered under the German flag. At the time of the purchase the vessel’s motor was working and the vessel was suitable for fishing. Its type book was in order and stamped by Germanischer Lloyd Classification Society. However, the information in the book did not correspond to reality, because the vessel was naturally unstable. The petitioner began fishing on the vessel in January 2008 and noted instantly that the vessel was significantly more unstable than his previous older vessel. Due to the unstable character, water entered the vessel and it was, on several occasions, at risk of sinking. In 2009, a new law entered into force in Ireland requiring all fishing vessels built after 1987 to pass a stability test performed by the Irish Maritime Administration. As a result, the Irish authorities prohibited the use of the vessel which the petitioner had bought. According to the preliminary hearing in the Netherlands, the vessel had always been overweight and it would never be seaworthy. The petitioner asserts to his rights in a transaction across EU countries, the failure of which has caused him to lose his livelihood and serious financial distress.

1254-2015.title: Petition 1254/2015: working conditions for professional drivers
1254-2015.description_full: The petitioner lodged a complaint with the German Bundestag’s petitions committee regarding lacking controls for cabotage in Germany, in which he requested that working conditions for professional drivers be improved. The petitioner claims that drivers working for foreign companies are often forced to sleep in their vehicles and that the pressure of their work can lead to them driving more aggressively or turning to alcohol. He also claims that such companies are using tactics including wage dumping and changing license plates in order to circumvent regulations. According to the petitioner, these practices are making it more difficult for German companies to compete in the market. The petition was sent to and investigated by the transport committee of the German government, who upheld that pay for professional drivers is decided by companies and that working conditions are checked by the police and the Bundesamt für Güterverkehr, with legal avenues available for complaints by drivers. The committee also reported that professional drivers in Germany receive fairly high wages (in a survey conducted in 2014), that more offences regarding working conditions are committed by German companies than foreign companies operating in Germany (in 2013), and that stricter rules are in force in Germany regarding obligatory resting times than at EU level. However, the committee points out that EU legislation does not prevent drivers from choosing to spend their resting time in their vehicles if they so desire. The German Bundestag has sent the petition to the European Parliament in the hope that a law could be introduced to prevent drivers from being able to choose to spend their rest time in their vehicles through enforcing fines for such actions. It is pointed out that such legislation would be more effective were it to be introduced at EU level, as simply introducing it in Germany might risk drivers travelling to neighbouring countries in order to rest legally in their vehicles.

1217-2014.title: Petition 1217/2014: passenger rights across different modes of transport
1217-2014.description_full: The petitioner suggests a number of improvements to passenger rights across different modes of transport, highlighting gaps and problems. Firstly, he refers to the lack of a joined-up approach to passenger rights and compensation for inter-modal journeys. He argues that, because there are no tickets combining two modes of transport (for example rail and air), passengers may needlessly miss connections, which, since the Regulation on Rail Passengers’ Rights and Obligations entered into force, no longer results in a full ticket refund. The petitioner argues that the Regulation should provide for a full refund where there is no longer a need for the ticket or where an alternative mode of transport must be used. He also points to the fact that many tickets are linked to a specific time of travel, causing problems with inter-modal travel. A late train, for instance, can mean missing the aeroplane and paying a large rebooking fee. The petitioner proposes that transport undertakings be required to allow free rebooking for the next available connection if the passenger can demonstrate that the connecting transport caused the delay. Secondly, he suggests that where tickets cannot be used because the passenger information system has given inaccurate data, transport companies should be required to pay compensation. Thirdly, the petitioner argues that, where a strike means that the journey cannot take place, tickets should be properly reimbursed (monthly season tickets should mean a refund of two single tickets per strike day). Fourthly, he complains about the practice of imposing and enforcing punitive charges or fines on passengers travelling without a valid ticket. In his opinion, most people caught without a ticket are either unable to pay at all, have simply forgotten to buy a ticket or have purchased the wrong ticket. He believes passengers should have the right to make good and simply purchase the correct ticket from a conductor and cannot see the economic argument for not employing conductors. Fifthly, the petitioner highlights problems with compensation where supplements have been paid for specific services that are then not performed. He cites, by way of example, the high-speed train link from Cologne to Frankfurt, which is 75 minutes faster than the slow line and costs 66% more, but where a 75-minute delay would result in a refund of just 25% of the ticket price. Similarly, Lufthansa Y fares are more expensive than B fares. When a B ticketholder takes a Y flight, he/she has to pay a surcharge. Yet, when a passenger with a Y ticket is put onto a B ticket flight, he/she receives no refund. The petitioner argues that the supplement should be reimbursed in full as the specific service is not being performed. Finally, the petitioner complains about the practice of some online travel agencies that allegedly do not confirm bookings until the last minute. According to the petitioner, these agencies deliberately undercut competitors to generate business, but do not actually have a ticket to offer. Instead, they hope to get a cheap ticket and adjust their booking fee accordingly to achieve the agreed price. Should they fail to do this, the customer faces last-minute cancellation or a last-minute and very expensive ticket purchase. The petitioner proposes therefore that waiting list bookings should be clearly indicated as such and that customers should be entitled to cancel the contract (with a small fee) up to the booking confirmation.

1205-2014.title: Petition 1205/2014: the payment of the television and radio licence fee in Germany
1205-2014.description_full: The petitioner is a pensioner and has a very low income. He lives in temporary accommodation. In Germany, the television and radio licence fee must be paid for in every dwelling. However, the petitioner argues that the shelter where he lives is not a full dwelling. He also claims that he does not own a television or radio. He has written to the German national broadcasting organisation about this, but was told that he must pay unless he has at his disposal a judicial decision stating that he does not have to pay. He asks the European Parliament for help.

2716-2013.title: Petition 2716/2013
2716-2013.description_full: The petitioner’s young daughter was abducted by her ex-partner (petitioner in Petitions 0979/2012 and 1060/2012) and taken to France. According to the petitioner, her ex-partner was aided in this by the organisation CEED (Conseil Européen des Enfants du Divorce - European Council for Children of Divorce). A French court subsequently found that the child was to remain with her father. The petitioner has not seen her child since May 2013. According to the petitioner, her ex-partner’s intention is to keep the child in France until such times as it no longer needs to be handed over on the basis of the Hague Convention. According to the petitioner, the German police and German politicians are working with the CEED organisation to prevent intensification of the debate on German family policy. The petitioner asks the European Parliament for help.

2252-2013.title: Petition 2252/2013
2252-2013.description_full: The petitioner states that his company, set up in Bulgaria, collaborated with a German company, beginning in 2003. The Bulgarian company works with materials supplied by the producers based on pre-defined models, established by means of agreements. Between 2012 and 2013, the German company began to significantly delay its payments, but nevertheless gave assurances that it was going to pay its debts. In June 2013, the German company submitted to the regional court an application for temporary insolvency, without informing its partner company. The German company placed another order, which should have been delivered by July 2013, but thereafter no longer answered the phone and refused to pay its debts. The petitioner accuses the German liquidator that it used the German legislation to deliberately obstruct the Bulgarian company’s activity.

0643-2013.title: Petition 0643/2013
0643-2013.description_full: The petitioner’s son has been taken into care by order of the Jugendamt in Darmstadt. As her son was aggressive and very difficult, he was placed in the Jugendamt’s Petra project. Here, however, he made no progress, so he was transferred to a different institution. Here too, no progress was made. In the meantime, the Jugendamt decided that the petitioner’s partner, who is from the USA, was the aggressor. The Jugendamt threatened to take the petitioner’s other 4 children into care too unless her partner left the house. The partner refused to do so, and the case came before the court, which ruled that the children did not need to be taken into care and that her son should be admitted to a different institution. Here his problem was correctly diagnosed and he is now making good progress. The petitioner wonders, in retrospect, why the Jugendamt’s opinion about her and her partner was never withdrawn and why the Jugendamt wished to have all her children taken into care. She is unhappy about the fact that the finger of guilt was pointed at her foreign partner and that her son’s problem was ignored. She calls for more scrutiny of the conduct of Jugendämter in Germany so that children and families receive the right assistance.
